title: Acquire peace
hookLine: Seraphim of Sarov: acquire a peaceful spirit, and thousands around you will be saved
tomorrow: grace before dinner, sure. but grace before a concert?

cards: A group chat blowing up at midnight. Two people sniping, everyone else picking a side or going quiet. Something has to change.
But which comes first: getting calm yourself, or stepping in? Calm inside first, or fix the room first? Two old Christian voices answer differently, and each has a strong case.

teach.b: The first voice is Seraphim of Sarov, a Russian monk who, tradition says, greeted every visitor with the words my joy. The saying linked to his name: acquire a peaceful spirit, and thousands around you will be saved.

Acquire is a marketplace verb: something gained and kept. In a conversation a friend wrote down, Seraphim calls the aim of the Christian life acquiring the Holy Spirit, the way a merchant acquires wealth.
His case: nobody can hand out what they haven't got. Peace travels from a person; a calm presence changes a room before anyone says a word.
Jesus says, “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you.” The second voice is the letter of James, and it has a warning that sounds aimed at nice words.

Someone is cold and hungry, and one of you says, “Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled,” but gives them nothing. “What doth it profit?” Its case: peace that stays inside while someone shivers isn't finished.
James doesn't throw peace out, though. He writes that “the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace.” And Seraphim's own door stood open to whoever came.
So the argument is about order, not about whether peace matters.
Inside first, says Seraphim. Out the door, says James.

how: Orthodox Christians honor Seraphim of Sarov as a saint, and Christians of other churches quote his saying about a peaceful spirit too.

p: a merchant's verb: gain and keep
depart in peace, but give nothing?

s: acquire a peaceful spirit means staying out of every conflict
Seraphim opened his door to whoever came; the peace is meant to reach thousands.
James warns about saying 'depart in peace' and giving nothing
what doth it profit? peace has to reach the cold and the hungry.
Seraphim's saying is a verse from the Bible

games.q: you side with James: help first, calm can wait. now state Seraphim's case at its strongest.
o: a person at peace changes the room before saying a word, and you can't hand out what you haven't got.
peace means keeping out of other people's problems entirely.
how you feel inside matters more than what you do, so action can wait forever.
games.why: Seraphim's best case: peace travels from a person, so acquire it first. James answers that peace with no help profits nothing. both keep peace; they argue about order.

practice: Close your eyes and let your breathing slow on its own. With each breath out, set down one thing you're carrying into the next hour: a hurry, a grudge, an argument still running in your head.
Near the end, let one person come to mind who could use that calm from you later today.

wordCard.voice: Acquire peace. Seraphim's teaching: gain a peaceful spirit, the way a merchant gains wealth, and it reaches the people around you.

orig.note: Greek for peace, the word in John 14:27, 'Peace I leave with you'.

carryVoice: For the road: thousands around you. Peace that starts inside, and doesn't stay there. That's day sixteen seventy-six.
